chunks: "The receiver doesn't get a clock, but it knows how long a bit should last because both sides agreed on the baud rate.
The line idles high, so the receiver just watches for a falling edge. That edge is the start bit and it's the only synchronisation it gets.
From that edge, it starts counting with its own clock.
It waits half a bit time, so it lands in the middle of the start bit, and checks the line is still low, which filters out glitches.
Then it waits one full bit time at a time, and each time it samples the line, so each sample lands in the middle of a data bit.
Sampling in the middle matters because that's the point farthest from both edges, where the signal is steadiest, so it has the most margin against clock error and noise.
After the data bits it samples the stop bit, which should be high. If it isn't, that's a framing error.
Then it goes back to waiting for the next falling edge, and everything restarts. The reason this works without a clock is that errors only accumulate over one frame.
Even if my clock is a couple of percent off, over ten bits the sampling point only slides a fraction of a bit, and then the next start edge resets it.
The limit is about 5% total mismatch for 8N1."
